definition.text: The simplest endogenous growth model, in which output is a linear function of capital, Y = AK.

facts.text: Its key feature is that capital has no diminishing returns, so growth need not fade to zero as in older models.
It is a Cobb–Douglas function where the output elasticity of capital equals 1.
Here K covers both physical and human capital, and A is a constant level of technology.
Textbooks mostly use it to introduce endogenous growth theory.

definition.text: The share of income saved that gives the highest level of consumption per person that can be kept up forever, as in the Solow–Swan model.

facts.text: Saving 100% leaves nothing to consume, and saving 0% lets capital wear out, so the best rate lies in between.
Edmund Phelps named it in 1961, applying 'do unto others' between generations.
It is reached where the marginal product of capital equals population growth plus depreciation.
An economy saving above this rate is dynamically inefficient: it could consume more both now and later by saving less.

definition.text: The increase in the number of people in a population.

facts.text: World population grew from 1 billion in 1800 to 8.3 billion in 2026, and now adds about 70 million people, or 0.84%, a year.
The global growth rate peaked at 2.2% a year in 1963 and has fallen since.
Better farming, sanitation and medicine drove growth; the demographic transition has slowed it in rich countries.
As of 2024 the UN projects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s.
Projections differ: the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation expects a peak of 9.73 billion in 2064, falling to 8.89 billion by 2100.
Together with rising consumption, it drives biodiversity loss and climate change through overuse of natural resources.
Population reduction is discussed as a sustainability strategy, though its potential is limited by respect for free life choices.

definition.text: A model in which a population's growth slows as it nears the carrying capacity, the largest population its environment can sustain.

facts.text: Most non-human populations follow a logistic rather than exponential path.
At carrying capacity the curve levels off, usually when the population has used up most of its natural resources.
Human population growth has followed a roughly linear trend over the last few decades.

definition.text: An economic model that explains long-run growth through capital accumulation, labour or population growth, and rising productivity from technological progress.

facts.text: Robert Solow and Trevor Swan developed it independently in 1956; Solow won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1987 for this work.
Its key assumption is diminishing returns to capital: each extra unit of capital adds less output than the one before.
Without technological progress, growth stops once new investment only replaces worn-out capital.
In the long run, lasting growth in income per person comes only from technological progress; saving and population growth change only levels.
It is called an exogenous growth model because it does not explain why technology improves.
It predicts poor countries should grow faster and catch up with rich ones, which is seldom seen in capital flows (Lucas' paradox).
It remains a common textbook model of long-run growth.
Output grows only through more capital, a larger population, or technology that raises total factor productivity.

title: Solow residual
article: Solow–Swan model#Variations in the effects of productivity

definition.text: The part of output growth left unexplained after accounting for capital accumulation, taken as a measure of total factor productivity growth.

facts.text: It is often credited entirely to technological progress but also includes lasting gains in how efficiently inputs are combined.
Economists use Solow's growth accounting to separate the effects of technology, capital and labour on growth.

definition.text: A 1992 version of the Solow–Swan model that adds human capital, such as education, as a factor of production.

facts.text: Poor countries have lower output and returns to capital because they have less human capital.
The estimated model explained 78% of the variation in income across countries.
Adding human capital lowers the estimate of the total factor productivity residual.

definition.text: The prediction that poor countries' incomes catch up with rich countries' if they save similar shares of output in physical and human capital.

facts.text: Since the 1950s output per worker in rich and poor countries has generally not converged, but poor countries that raised their saving rates have converged.
Japan converged with rich countries after raising its saving rates in the 1950s and 1960s.
Endogenous growth theories are criticized for failing to explain the conditional convergence seen in the data.
